comparison: Perfect agreement on phylogenetic signal findings (C45-C50). Both OpenEval and peer reviewers find the Mantel test results and statistical methods appropriate and convincing, with no challenges raised.

Strong agreement on dataset compilation and descriptive statistics (C22-C38). Both accept the host distribution data and phylogenetic patterns without challenge. Peer reviewers implicitly validate the dataset through acceptance of robustness testing.
Strong agreement on biogeographic findings (C70-C75, C99-C100). Both find the geographic diversity hotspots in East Asia and Europe well-supported and consistent with recent origination scenario.

Both express uncertainty about ALE reconciliation results (C51-C57). OpenEval notes high proportion of time-inconsistent switches undermines confidence; peer reviewer explicitly identifies the failure of dated ALE model as a significant methodological limitation.
Agreement on alpha vs. beta coronavirus differences (C64-C69, C96-C98). Both accept the contrasting patterns between genera without challenge, supporting the overall host-switching framework.

Divergent confidence levels on main conclusions (C76-C80, C113, C119). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN due to indirect evidence and inability to date origination; peer reviewers rate as SUPPORTED, finding evidence 'convincing' and 'conceptually robust.'

Divergent assessment of marker limitations (C105-C108). OpenEval finds the palmprint marker validation SUPPORTED with honest acknowledgment of limitations; peer reviewer rates as UNCERTAIN, explicitly concerned that single marker and lack of resolution for recent divergences could affect conclusions.
Agreement on preferential within-order host switching patterns (C83-C86, C115). Both accept that host switches occur preferentially between closely related species within mammalian orders.

Partial overlap on star phylogeny ALE results (C58-C60). OpenEval finds this approach well-supported for testing preferential switches; peer reviewer's uncertainty about time-inconsistent transfers applies more broadly to all ALE analyses.

Partial overlap on human intermediate host role (C61-C62 vs C89-C90, C120). OpenEval supports star phylogeny findings; peer reviewers explicitly affirm humans as intermediate hosts with significant role in spillovers.

Agreement on rarity of bat spillovers (C87-C88). Both OpenEval and peer reviewers support this finding, with peer reviewer explicitly highlighting 'the rarity of spillovers from bats to other species.'
Agreement on frequent bat-to-human switches (C89-C90 vs C61-C62, C120). Both support the finding that humans act as intermediate hosts with relatively higher likelihood of spillovers from bats.

Agreement on methodological contribution regarding codiversification overestimation (C81-C82, C118). Both recognize the study's contribution to showing that topology-based methods may overestimate codiversification.

Agreement on predictions about future spread (C101-C103, C116, C121). Both accept these as reasonable extrapolations from the host-switching findings, with peer reviewer affirming 'potential for rapid additional spreading.'

Agreement on robustness of sensitivity analyses (C110, C112). Both accept the recombination and sampling bias tests, though peer reviewer notes residual uncertainty about single marker generalizability.
Agreement on alpha/beta genus differences in geographic origins (C96-C100). Both accept these subclade-specific patterns as part of the overall host-switching framework.
Agreement on predictions and forward-looking interpretations (C116, C121). Both accept these as reasonable extrapolations about future coronavirus spread based on host-switching patterns.
Divergent confidence on main conclusions (C113, C119). OpenEval supports summary conclusions with caveats; peer reviewers find overall conclusions 'convincing' despite methodological limitations.
Agreement on geographic origins and diversity hotspots (C99-C100). Both accept the biogeographic findings about East Asian and European origins.

Agreement on conservation recommendations (C117, C95). Both implicitly or explicitly support conservation-based mitigation strategies following from bat origin and human-mediated transmission findings.
Agreement on conservation implications (C95). Both accept that rare bat spillovers support conservation-based approaches to reducing human-wildlife contact.
Agreement on methodological conclusion about codiversification (C118). Both recognize the study's contribution to showing overestimation of virus-host codiversification in prior work.
Agreement on human intermediate host role (C120). Both support the interpretation that humans play a significant role as intermediate hosts in coronavirus evolution.
Agreement on within-order transmission patterns (C115). Both accept that host switches occur preferentially within mammalian orders including humans and domesticated animals.

OpenEval evaluates background/introduction claims (C1-C13) as SUPPORTED with appropriate citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these contextual claims about coronavirus biology and taxonomy.
OpenEval evaluates literature review and motivation claims (C14-C21) as SUPPORTED. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these claims about prior work and methodological challenges.
OpenEval evaluates network visualization findings (C42-C44) as SUPPORTED but primarily qualitative. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these specific network analysis claims.

OpenEval rates claims contrasting prior hypotheses with current findings (C92-C94) as UNCERTAIN, noting unresolved tension between species-level and deeper evolutionary patterns. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.
